deep.lede: Each Gospel gives Jesus different last words. Mark and Matthew have a cry of abandonment, Luke a prayer of trust, John a declaration of completion. No passage shows more clearly that the evangelists were interpreters, not just recorders.

sections.heading: Mark: the cry from Psalm 22
sections.body:
Mark preserves the cry in Aramaic and then translates it: {mk 15:34 Ἐλωῒ ἐλωῒ λεμὰ σαβαχθάνι} (“Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani”), {mk 15:34 Ὁ θεός μου ὁ θεός μου εἰς τί ἐγκατέλιπές με} (“My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”). It is the opening line of Psalm 22, whose details Mark has been tracing throughout the crucifixion. Readers have argued for centuries over whether the cry is pure desolation or whether quoting the first line evokes the whole psalm, which ends in vindication. Mark does not say.

Matthew keeps the cry but gives the Hebrew form {mt 27:46 Ἠλὶ ἠλὶ}, which makes the bystanders' mishearing as a call to Elijah (*Ēlias*) easier to understand. A detail like this suggests Matthew knew the languages involved.

sections.heading: Luke: a different psalm
sections.body:
Luke leaves out the cry of abandonment entirely. In its place Jesus prays Psalm 31:5: {lk 23:46 Πάτερ εἰς χεῖράς σου παρατίθεμαι τὸ πνεῦμά μου} (“Father, into your hands I commit my spirit”). This was a traditional Jewish evening prayer, and Luke adds the address “Father”, so that Jesus' first recorded words in the Gospel (2:49, “my Father's house”) and his last both speak of the Father.

Luke's centurion also says something different. Mark's says {mk 15:39 Ἀληθῶς οὗτος ὁ ἄνθρωπος υἱὸς θεοῦ ἦν} (“truly this man was God's Son”), the first human being in Mark to say so with understanding. Luke's says {lk 23:47 Ὄντως ὁ ἄνθρωπος οὗτος δίκαιος ἦν} (“surely this man was **innocent**” or “righteous”). Luke's interest, here as at Pilate's trial, is in Jesus' innocence.

sections.heading: John: “It is finished”
sections.body: John's Jesus remains in control to the end. He speaks {jn 19:28 εἰδὼς ὁ Ἰησοῦς ὅτι ἤδη πάντα τετέλεσται} (“knowing that all was now completed”), and his final word is the same verb: {jn 19:30 Τετέλεσται} (“it is finished”, or “accomplished”). John doesn't say he “breathed his last”, as the Synoptics do ({mk 15:37 ἐξέπνευσεν}); he says {jn 19:30 παρέδωκεν τὸ πνεῦμα} (“he handed over the spirit”). The death is presented as an act Jesus performs, not something that happens to him.

sections.heading: Signs: the veil, the earthquake, the open tombs
sections.body:
In Mark the moment of death is followed by one sign: {mk 15:38 τὸ καταπέτασμα τοῦ ναοῦ ἐσχίσθη εἰς δύο} (“the curtain of the temple was torn in two”). The verb *schizō* appeared once before in Mark, when the heavens were {mk 1:10 σχιζομένους} (“torn open”) at the baptism. The two tearings frame the Gospel.

Matthew adds an earthquake and something no other Gospel reports: {mt 27:52 πολλὰ σώματα τῶν κεκοιμημένων ἁγίων ἠγέρθησαν} (“many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep were raised”). Even many conservative commentators read this as apocalyptic imagery from Ezekiel 37 rather than as a report of events. Others take Matthew at his word: a real, if mysterious, event, a first sign of the general resurrection. Luke moves the veil earlier, to just before Jesus dies ({lk 23:45 ἐσχίσθη δὲ τὸ καταπέτασμα τοῦ ναοῦ μέσον}), and John omits it. In John, the sign is from Jesus' own body: {jn 19:34 ἐξῆλθεν εὐθὺς αἷμα καὶ ὕδωρ} (“at once blood and water came out”).

deep.lede: All four Gospels agree that women went to Jesus' tomb on the first day of the week and found it empty. They disagree about almost everything else: how many women, how many angels, who saw what, and what the women did next. The disagreements are among the most studied in New Testament scholarship. Traditional harmonies, from Augustine on, fit the accounts together (one angel speaking does not exclude a second), and many readers see the untidy variety as a mark of independent witnesses rather than invention.

sections.heading: Mark's ending in fear
sections.body:
In Mark a {mk 16:5 νεανίσκον} (“young man”) in white tells the women {mk 16:6 ἠγέρθη οὐκ ἔστιν ὧδε} (“he has been raised; he is not here”) and sends them to tell {mk 16:7 τοῖς μαθηταῖς αὐτοῦ καὶ τῷ Πέτρῳ} (“his disciples, **and Peter**”), naming the disciple who denied him. Then comes the most startling sentence in the Gospels: the women flee and say nothing to anyone, {mk 16:8 ἐφοβοῦντο γάρ} (“for they were afraid”).

In the oldest manuscripts, Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, Mark ends there, on the Greek conjunction *gar*. Later scribes added at least two different endings to fill the gap, and the site marks those verses as disputed text. Whether Mark meant to end this way, or lost his last page, is still debated. Many scholars now think the abrupt ending is deliberate, leaving readers to finish the story themselves. A minority, along with many traditional readers, defend the longer ending as part of the Gospel.

sections.heading: Matthew: an earthquake and joy
sections.body: Matthew turns the scene into an apocalyptic event: {mt 28:2 σεισμὸς ἐγένετο μέγας} (“there was a great earthquake”), and an angel {mt 28:2 ἀπεκύλισε τὸν λίθον καὶ ἐκάθητο ἐπάνω αὐτοῦ} (“rolled back the stone and sat on it”). Matthew also reverses Mark's ending. The women leave {mt 28:8 μετὰ φόβου καὶ χαρᾶς μεγάλης} (“with fear and great joy”) and run to tell the disciples. The fear stays, but joy is added and silence becomes proclamation.

sections.heading: Luke: two men, and a question
sections.body: Luke has {lk 24:4 ἄνδρες δύο} (“two men”) in dazzling clothes. They ask {lk 24:5 Τί ζητεῖτε τὸν ζῶντα μετὰ τῶν νεκρῶν} (“why do you look for the living among the dead?”) and tell the women to remember Jesus' words {lk 24:6 ἐν τῇ Γαλιλαίᾳ} (“in Galilee”). Mark had said the disciples would see Jesus *in* Galilee; Luke's resurrection appearances all happen around Jerusalem, so Galilee becomes a place remembered, not a destination. When the women report, the apostles think it {lk 24:11 λῆρος} (“nonsense”). It is a striking admission for a Gospel to make about its own heroes.

sections.heading: Peter and the Beloved Disciple
sections.body:
Luke 24:12 and John 20 share an unusual cluster of wording. In both, a disciple runs to the tomb and {lk 24:12 παρακύψας βλέπει τὰ ὀθόνια} / {jn 20:5 παρακύψας βλέπει κείμενα τὰ ὀθόνια} (“stooping down, he sees the linen cloths”). In John the Beloved Disciple {jn 20:4 προέδραμεν τάχιον τοῦ Πέτρου} (“outran Peter”) and, once inside, {jn 20:8 εἶδεν καὶ ἐπίστευσεν} (“saw and believed”).

Luke 24:12 is missing from Codex Bezae, so Westcott and Hort treated it as a later harmonization with John. The verse is in P75, and most modern editions accept it. If it is original, it is among the strongest evidence that Luke and John drew on a shared tradition, or that one knew the other.

deep.lede: The first person to see the risen Jesus, according to Matthew, John and the added ending of Mark, was a woman, or a group of women. That fact is all the more striking because women's testimony counted for little in the ancient world, and Paul's list of witnesses (1 Corinthians 15:5–8) does not mention them at all.

sections.heading: Matthew: feet held and worship
sections.body: Matthew's appearance is brief and physical. Jesus meets the women with an ordinary greeting, {mt 28:9 Χαίρετε} (“Greetings!”), and they {mt 28:9 ἐκράτησαν αὐτοῦ τοὺς πόδας καὶ προσεκύνησαν αὐτῷ} (“took hold of his feet and worshipped him”). Holding his feet answers any suggestion that they saw a ghost. Jesus then repeats the angel's message almost word for word, with one change: the disciples are now {mt 28:10 τοῖς ἀδελφοῖς μου} (“my **brothers**”). The ones who fled are not disowned.

sections.heading: John: the gardener
sections.body:
John tells one of the most carefully crafted recognition scenes in ancient literature. Mary Magdalene, weeping, is asked {jn 20:15 τίνα ζητεῖς} (“whom are you looking for?”), the same question Jesus asked the first disciples (1:38) and the arresting soldiers (18:4). She mistakes him for {jn 20:15 ὁ κηπουρός} (“the gardener”). Then he says one word, her name, {jn 20:16 Μαριάμ}, and she knows him, as Jesus had said the sheep know the shepherd's voice when he “calls his own sheep by name” (10:3).

His next words are puzzling: {jn 20:17 Μή μου ἅπτου} (“do not cling to me”, or “stop holding on to me”). The present tense suggests stopping an action already under way, so this is no ban on touch. Thomas will be invited to touch the wounds a week later. Jesus' presence is about to take a new form, {jn 20:17 Ἀναβαίνω πρὸς τὸν πατέρα μου καὶ πατέρα ὑμῶν} (“I am ascending to my Father and your Father”).

sections.heading: Mark's longer ending
sections.body: The added ending of Mark (16:9–20) summarizes appearances that look like a digest of the other Gospels. It begins {mk 16:9 ἐφάνη πρῶτον Μαρίᾳ τῇ Μαγδαληνῇ} (“he appeared first to Mary Magdalene”), then mentions two travellers in the country (much like Luke's Emmaus story) and a commissioning of the eleven. Most scholars date it to the early second century. Its wording is uncharacteristic of Mark, and it is absent from the earliest manuscripts. Its defenders point out that it stands in the great majority of manuscripts and that Irenaeus quoted it around 180 CE. The site's data marks it as a later addition, but it is a valuable early witness to how Christians combined the four Gospels.

deep.lede: Each Gospel ends with Jesus commissioning his followers, and each ending sums up its Gospel. Matthew's is on a mountain in Galilee, Luke's in a room in Jerusalem, John's behind locked doors. Placed together, they show four theologies of mission, and very little shared wording.

sections.heading: Matthew: the mountain and the Great Commission
sections.body:
On a Galilean mountain, which recalls the Sermon on the Mount and Moses on Sinai, the eleven worship, {mt 28:17 οἱ δὲ ἐδίστασαν} (“but some doubted”). The Greek can mean that some of them doubted, or that all did. Matthew includes the doubt, even at the end.

The commission is {mt 28:19 μαθητεύσατε πάντα τὰ ἔθνη} (“make disciples of all nations”), reversing the earlier instruction to go only to “the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (10:6). The triple baptismal formula {mt 28:19 εἰς τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ πατρὸς καὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ καὶ τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος} is unique in the Gospels and probably reflects the practice of Matthew's church; traditional readers take it as Jesus' own command, which the church then followed. The final promise, {mt 28:20 ἐγὼ μεθ ὑμῶν εἰμι} (“I am with you”), echoes Emmanuel, “God with us”, from the first chapter (1:23).

sections.heading: Luke: flesh and fish
sections.body:
Luke's Jesus insists on his physical body: {lk 24:39 ψηλαφήσατέ με καὶ ἴδετε ὅτι πνεῦμα σάρκα καὶ ὀστέα οὐκ ἔχει} (“touch me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones”). Then he eats {lk 24:42 ἰχθύος ὀπτοῦ μέρος} (“a piece of broiled fish”). Luke seems to be answering people who said the disciples had seen only a ghost.

The commission is framed the way Acts will tell the story: {lk 24:47 μετάνοιαν καὶ ἄφεσιν ἁμαρτιῶν εἰς πάντα τὰ ἔθνη ἀρξάμενοι ἀπὸ Ἰερουσαλήμ} (“repentance and forgiveness of sins to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem”). Luke's second volume begins exactly where this verse points.

sections.heading: John: breath and forgiveness
sections.body:
In John the risen Jesus comes through locked doors and says {jn 20:19 Εἰρήνη ὑμῖν} (“peace be with you”). Then {jn 20:22 ἐνεφύσησεν} (“he breathed on them”). The same rare verb appears in the Greek Old Testament when God breathes life into Adam (Genesis 2:7) and into the dry bones (Ezekiel 37:9). John's Pentecost happens on Easter evening, as a new creation.

The saying about forgiving sins, {jn 20:23 ἄν τινων ἀφῆτε τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἀφέωνται αὐτοῖς} (“if you forgive anyone's sins, they are forgiven”), parallels Matthew's “binding and loosing” (16:19, 18:18) but uses different words. That points to a shared tradition reached by separate paths, not to copying.

sections.heading: Mark's added commission
sections.body: The longer ending of Mark has its own version: {mk 16:15 κηρύξατε τὸ εὐαγγέλιον πάσῃ τῇ κτίσει} (“preach the gospel to all creation”), followed by promises of signs including handling snakes and drinking poison. The wording is closer to a blend of Matthew and Luke than to anything in Mark, which is one of several reasons scholars consider these verses a later addition.

deep.lede: Jesus enters Jerusalem on a donkey in all four Gospels, a rare case in which John and the Synoptics clearly tell the same event. How many animals there were, what the crowd shouted, and who understood what was happening differ from Gospel to Gospel, and the differences show each writer's method.

sections.heading: Matthew's two animals
sections.body:
Mark has one {mk 11:2 πῶλον} (“colt”), and Jesus sits on it. Matthew has the disciples find {mt 21:2 ὄνον δεδεμένην καὶ πῶλον μετ αὐτῆς} (“a donkey tied, and a colt with her”) and says Jesus {mt 21:7 ἐπεκάθισεν ἐπάνω αὐτῶν} (“sat on them”). The reason is the prophecy Matthew quotes, Zechariah 9:9: {mt 21:5 ἐπὶ ὄνον καὶ ἐπὶ πῶλον υἱὸν ὑποζυγίου} (“on a donkey, and on a colt, the foal of a donkey”).

Hebrew poetry often says the same thing twice in parallel lines; Zechariah means one animal. On the critical reading, Matthew takes the lines literally and adds a second donkey. Critics see Matthew shaping the story to fit the text; defenders note that an unbroken colt might well be brought with its mother. Either way, the change follows from the prophecy he cites, {mt 21:4 ἵνα πληρωθῇ τὸ ῥηθὲν} (“so that what was spoken might be fulfilled”).

sections.heading: What the crowd shouted
sections.body:
All four Gospels quote Psalm 118:26, {mk 11:9 Εὐλογημένος ὁ ἐρχόμενος ἐν ὀνόματι κυρίου} (“blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord”), but each adds a different interpretation:

**Mark**: {mk 11:10 Εὐλογημένη ἡ ἐρχομένη βασιλεία τοῦ πατρὸς ἡμῶν Δαυίδ} (“blessed is the coming kingdom of our father David”).

**Luke**: puts the king inside the psalm verse, {lk 19:38 ὁ ἐρχόμενος βασιλεὺς} (“the **king** who comes”), and drops the Aramaic *Hosanna*, which his Gentile readers would not know. He adds {lk 19:38 ἐν οὐρανῷ εἰρήνη} (“peace in heaven”), echoing the angels' song at the birth (2:14).

**John**: {jn 12:13 ὁ βασιλεὺς τοῦ Ἰσραήλ} (“the King of Israel”), and only John mentions {jn 12:13 τὰ βαΐα τῶν φοινίκων} (“palm branches”), which is where Palm Sunday gets its name.

sections.heading: Stones and remembering
sections.body:
Luke adds a short exchange. Some Pharisees ask Jesus to rebuke his disciples, and he answers {lk 19:40 ἐὰν οὗτοι σιωπήσουσιν οἱ λίθοι κράξουσιν} (“if these are silent, the stones will cry out”). This may echo Habakkuk 2:11.

John adds a comment that is valuable for understanding how the Gospels were written: {jn 12:16 ταῦτα οὐκ ἔγνωσαν αὐτοῦ οἱ μαθηταὶ τὸ πρῶτον} (“his disciples did not understand these things at first”). Only after Jesus was glorified did they remember the scriptures. John admits openly what scholars infer about all four Gospels: the events were understood, and narrated, in light of the resurrection.

deep.lede: Jesus overturning tables in the Temple is in all four Gospels, but John places it at the **start** of Jesus' ministry, and the Synoptics in his last week. It is the largest chronological disagreement between John and the Synoptics, and how one explains it shows how one thinks the Gospels work.

sections.heading: The act
sections.body:
In Mark, Jesus {mk 11:15 ἤρξατο ἐκβάλλειν τοὺς πωλοῦντας καὶ τοὺς ἀγοράζοντας} (“began to drive out those selling and buying”) and overturns the tables of the money changers. Only Mark adds {mk 11:16 οὐκ ἤφιεν ἵνα τις διενέγκῃ σκεῦος διὰ τοῦ ἱεροῦ} (“he would not let anyone carry a vessel through the temple”), in effect halting the Temple's daily business. Matthew and Luke both drop this verse, perhaps because it seemed implausible or too disruptive.

John's version is the most violent: Jesus makes {jn 2:15 φραγέλλιον ἐκ σχοινίων} (“a whip of cords”), drives out the sheep and cattle, and {jn 2:15 ἐξέχεεν τὰ κέρματα} (“poured out the coins”).

sections.heading: “For all the nations”
sections.body:
Mark quotes Isaiah 56:7 in full: {mk 11:17 Ὁ οἶκός μου οἶκος προσευχῆς κληθήσεται πᾶσιν τοῖς ἔθνεσιν} (“my house shall be called a house of prayer **for all the nations**”). The trading probably took place in the Court of the Gentiles, the only part of the Temple open to non-Jews, so the phrase matters. Matthew ({mt 21:13 οἶκος προσευχῆς κληθήσεται}) and Luke ({lk 19:46 οἶκος προσευχῆς}) both omit “for all the nations”. This is a minor agreement of omission. A common explanation is that both wrote after the Temple's destruction in 70 CE, when the promise about the Temple's future no longer made sense. Those who date Matthew and Luke earlier see a simple abbreviation.

John uses different words altogether: {jn 2:16 μὴ ποιεῖτε τὸν οἶκον τοῦ πατρός μου οἶκον ἐμπορίου} (“do not make my Father's house a house of trade”), which echoes Zechariah 14:21 rather than Isaiah.

sections.heading: One event or two?
sections.body:
In John, the Temple action leads to a riddle: {jn 2:19 Λύσατε τὸν ναὸν τοῦτον καὶ ἐν τρισὶν ἡμέραις ἐγερῶ αὐτόν} (“destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up”), which the narrator explains: {jn 2:21 ἐκεῖνος δὲ ἔλεγεν περὶ τοῦ ναοῦ τοῦ σώματος αὐτοῦ} (“he was speaking of the temple of his body”). In Mark, a garbled version of the same saying comes up at the trial (14:58), from false witnesses.

There are three main explanations. Traditional harmonizers propose two cleansings, one early and one late. Most critical scholars think there was one, which the Synoptics placed late because their structure has only one trip to Jerusalem, and which John moved to the start as a theological overture. A minority argue that John's dating is historically more likely. The data on this site can't settle the question, but it shows how little wording the two accounts share.

deep.lede: A woman pours expensive perfume on Jesus. The story is told four times, and the versions overlap in a tangle that has puzzled readers since antiquity. Mark and Matthew have an unnamed woman anointing his head in Bethany; John has Mary of Bethany anointing his feet; Luke has a forgiven sinner in Galilee. Is it one event, two, or three?

sections.heading: Mark: a woman to be remembered
sections.body:
In Mark the woman is unnamed. She breaks an {mk 14:3 ἀλάβαστρον μύρου νάρδου πιστικῆς πολυτελοῦς} (“alabaster flask of very costly ointment of pure nard”) and pours it on Jesus' **head**, the way kings were anointed in the Old Testament. Onlookers complain that it could have been sold for {mk 14:5 ἐπάνω δηναρίων τριακοσίων} (“more than three hundred denarii”), about a year's wages for a laborer.

Jesus reinterprets her act: {mk 14:8 προέλαβεν μυρίσαι τὸ σῶμά μου εἰς τὸν ἐνταφιασμόν} (“she has anointed my body beforehand for burial”). He then makes a promise found in no other story: {mk 14:9 ὃ ἐποίησεν αὕτη λαληθήσεται εἰς μνημόσυνον αὐτῆς} (“what she has done will be told in memory of her”). The irony, often noted by feminist scholars, is that her name was not preserved.

sections.heading: Matthew: the disciples complain
sections.body: Matthew follows Mark closely; the alignment shows about 60% shared wording. He sharpens one detail: Mark's vague {mk 14:4 τινες} (“some”) become {mt 26:8 οἱ μαθηταὶ} (“the disciples”). This is unusual, because Matthew more often softens Mark's criticism of the Twelve.

sections.heading: John: Mary, the feet, and Judas
sections.body:
John's version has strikingly specific links to Mark: the same rare phrase {jn 12:3 μύρου νάρδου πιστικῆς}, and the same sum, {jn 12:5 τριακοσίων δηναρίων}. The adjective *pistikos*, probably “genuine” or “pure”, is almost unknown in Greek outside these two passages, which makes independent use by both writers unlikely.

Yet John's woman is Mary, sister of Lazarus, and she anoints the **feet** and {jn 12:3 ἐξέμαξεν ταῖς θριξὶν αὐτῆς} (“wiped them with her hair”). That gesture belongs to Luke's quite different story of a sinful woman, who {lk 7:38 ταῖς θριξὶν τῆς κεφαλῆς αὐτῆς ἐξέμασσεν} (“wiped them with the hair of her head”). The complainer in John is named: {jn 12:4 Ἰούδας ὁ Ἰσκαριώτης}, whom John alone calls a thief who {jn 12:6 τὰ βαλλόμενα ἐβάσταζεν} (“used to take what was put in” the common purse).

sections.heading: How did the stories merge?
sections.body:
The most common scholarly explanation is that oral tradition blended two stories: a Bethany anointing on the head before the Passion, and a Galilean sinful woman weeping on Jesus' feet. John's version shows features of both. Many traditional readers keep the events apart: a sinful woman in Galilee earlier in the ministry, and Mary of Bethany days before the Passion, with Mark and Matthew placing the Bethany meal just before the betrayal for thematic reasons.

Later Western tradition went further. Pope Gregory the Great (591 CE) identified the sinful woman of Luke 7 with Mary of Bethany and with Mary Magdalene, producing the penitent-prostitute Magdalene of Western art. No Gospel makes that link. The Catholic Church quietly set the identification aside in its 1969 liturgical calendar.
